### Ticket Type

🐛 Bug Report (Something isn't working)

### Environment & System Info

```Shell
- LeRobot version: 0.6.2 (main @ 58314984)
- Platform: Linux-6.18.33.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2-x86_64-with-glibc2.39
- Python version: 3.12.3
- Huggingface Hub version: 1.33.0
- Transformers version: 5.5.4
- Numpy version: 2.2.6
- PyTorch version: 2.11.0+cpu
- Is PyTorch built with CUDA support?: False
- Using GPU in script?: No (CPU only)
```

### Description

When an action chunk runs past the end of an episode, the dataset repeats the last action and flags those steps in `action_is_pad`. `PI0Policy.forward` never reads `action_is_pad`: both reduction paths use a plain `losses.mean()`. So padded steps are trained toward the frozen final pose and receive the same gradient as real steps.

SmolVLA (#3434) and ACT / Diffusion / MultiTaskDiT (#3442) already mask these steps and normalize over valid entries. pi0 was not covered, likely because it never applied the mask, so the "mask then mean" search in #3377 did not find it.

### Context & Reproduction

A unit test that calls the real `PI0Policy.forward` with stubbed model outputs (per-step losses `[1, 2, 3, 4]`, last two steps padded in one sample):

| | loss | grad on padded steps |
|---|---|---|
| current `main` | 2.5 (same as with no padding) | 1/16, same as valid steps |
| expected | 26/12 ≈ 2.17 (valid entries only) | 0 |

Batches without `action_is_pad` give the same result before and after.

### Relevant logs or stack trace

```Shell

```

### Checklist

- [x] I have searched existing tickets to ensure this isn't a duplicate.
- [x] I am using the latest version of the `main` branch.
- [x] I have verified this is not an environment-specific problem.

### Additional Info / Workarounds

openpi has the same behavior and an open report about it (Physical-Intelligence/openpi#681), where users describe the robot freezing where episodes usually end. So this changes pi0's loss relative to openpi when padding is present. Happy to put it behind a config flag if you'd prefer to keep exact parity.

openpi issue: https://github.com/Physical-Intelligence/openpi/issues/681

A PR with the fix and tests will follow shortly. From reading the code, pi05 has the same gap; I'll send a separate PR for it.

### Description

Two code paths in moveit_core/planning_scene/src/planning_scene.cpp iterate over subframe_poses.size() and access subframe_names[I] without checking whether the two vectors have equal lengths.

The affected locations are:

- Lines 1616–1620: attached collision object processing.
- Lines 1925–1933: collision object ADD processing.

The relevant code is:

for (std::size_t i = 0; i < object.subframe_poses.size(); ++i)
{
    utilities::poseMsgToEigen(object.subframe_poses[i], subframe_pose);
    std::string name = object.subframe_names[i];
    subframes[name] = subframe_pose;
}

When subframe_poses.size() > subframe_names.size(), the access to subframe_names[i] is out of bounds, resulting in undefined behavior.

A similar code path in moveit_core/robot_state/src/conversions.cpp (around line 271) already performs an explicit size consistency check:


if (aco.object.subframe_poses.size() != aco.object.subframe_names.size())
{
    RCLCPP_ERROR(...);
    return;
}


The corresponding validation appears to be missing from the two PlanningScene code paths.

Suggested fix: Validate the lengths of subframe_poses and subframe_names before accessing either vector, and reject malformed messages without modifying the planning scene.

This issue is based on source-code inspection. Runtime reproduction is pending.

2. Add one valid pose to subframe_poses.
3. Leave subframe_names empty.
4. Submit the message through the PlanningScene collision object ADD processing path.
5. Run the test with AddressSanitizer or a bounds-checking STL configuration to detect the potential out-of-bounds access.

The attached collision object path should be tested separately with the same mismatched subframe arrays.

The operation should reject inconsistent subframe arrays and report an error without accessing memory outside the vector.

### Actual behavior

new_candidates.body:
### Description

Description

In moveit_core/collision_detection/src/world.cpp, two methods modify the internal state of a world object without first calling ensureUnique():

- World::moveShapesInObject() (around line 266)
- World::setSubframesOfObject() (around line 369)

The ensureUnique() helper implements copy-on-write protection by creating an independent object instance when the existing object is shared.

A similar method, World::moveShapeInObject(), correctly calls ensureUnique(it->second) before modifying the object's shape poses:

ensureUnique(it->second);
ASSERT_ISOMETRY(shape_pose)
it->second->shape_poses_[i] = shape_pose;
it->second->global_shape_poses_[i] = it->second->pose_ * shape_pose;


However, moveShapesInObject() directly modifies the stored object:

for (std::size_t i = 0; i < shape_poses.size(); ++i)
{
  ASSERT_ISOMETRY(shape_poses[i])
  it->second->shape_poses_[i] = shape_poses[i];
  it->second->global_shape_poses_[i] = it->second->pose_ * shape_poses[i];
}


Similarly, setSubframesOfObject() updates the object directly:

obj_pair->second->subframe_poses_ = subframe_poses;
obj_pair->second->global_subframe_poses_ = subframe_poses;
updateGlobalPosesInternal(obj_pair->second, false, true);

Neither method calls ensureUnique() before modifying the object.

If multiple World instances share the same underlying object, these operations may unintentionally modify the state visible to other world instances, violating copy-on-write isolation.

Suggested Fix

Call ensureUnique() before mutating the object in both methods, consistent with moveShapeInObject().

Add regression tests verifying that changes made to one World instance do not affect another World instance sharing the original object.

### ROS Distro

Humble

### OS and version

Ubuntu 22.04

### Source or binary build?

Source

### If binary, which release version?

_No response_

### If source, which branch?

_No response_

### Which RMW are you using?

None

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a collision_detection::World instance.
2. Add a collision object containing multiple shapes and a subframe.
3. Copy the World instance so that both Worlds initially share the same underlying object.
4. Record the shape poses and subframe transforms in the copied World.
5. Call moveShapesInObject() on the original World with updated shape poses.
6. Check whether the corresponding shape poses in the copied World have also changed.
7. Repeat the experiment using setSubframesOfObject() to update the subframe transforms.
8. Compare the states of both World instances after each operation.

These are proposed regression-test steps. The suspected cross-World state modification has not yet been verified at runtime.

### Expected behavior

When a World instance is copied, the two instances may initially share object storage for efficiency.

However, modifying the shape poses or subframe transforms in one World should not affect the corresponding objects in the other World.

Both moveShapesInObject() and setSubframesOfObject() should preserve copy-on-write isolation, consistently with other World mutation methods.

### Actual behavior

Source inspection shows that moveShapesInObject() and setSubframesOfObject() directly modify the stored World object without calling ensureUnique().

Other World mutation methods, such as moveShapeInObject(), explicitly call ensureUnique() before modifying object state.

If the object is shared by multiple World instances, the missing copy-on-write protection may cause modifications in one World to become visible in another.

This behavior has not yet been confirmed with a runtime regression test.

new_candidates.body:
### Description

In PlanningScene::processCollisionObjectMove(), the collision object's global pose is updated before validating the number of shape poses provided in the MOVE message.

Affected file:

moveit_core/planning_scene/src/planning_scene.cpp

The object pose is updated first (around line 1976):

const Eigen::Isometry3d object_frame_transform =
    world_to_object_header_transform * header_to_pose_transform;

world_->setObjectPose(object.id, object_frame_transform);


However, the number of supplied shape poses is validated only afterward (around lines 1979–1989):

if (!object.primitive_poses.empty() ||
    !object.mesh_poses.empty() ||
    !object.plane_poses.empty())
{
  auto world_object = world_->getObject(object.id);

  std::size_t shape_size =
      object.primitive_poses.size() +
      object.mesh_poses.size() +
      object.plane_poses.size();

  if (shape_size != world_object->shape_poses_.size())
  {
    RCLCPP_ERROR(
        getLogger(),
        "Move operation for object '%s' must have same number of geometry poses. Cannot move.",
        object.id.c_str());
    return false;
  }
}

Consequently, if the shape pose count does not match, the function returns false, but the global object pose has already been modified.

This creates a partial state update: the operation reports failure while the PlanningScene may retain a changed collision object pose.

This can cause inconsistencies between the caller's understanding of the operation result and the collision world state.

Suggested Fix

Validate the supplied shape pose count before calling world_->setObjectPose()

Ideally, all MOVE request validation should be completed before applying any modification to the collision world.

A regression test should verify that a rejected MOVE request leaves both the global object pose and the individual shape poses unchanged.

### ROS Distro

Humble

### OS and version

Ubuntu 22.04

### Source or binary build?

Source

### If binary, which release version?

_No response_

### If source, which branch?

_No response_

### Which RMW are you using?

None

### Steps to Reproduce

Proposed reproduction steps (not yet executed):

1. Create a PlanningScene with a valid robot model.
2. Add a collision object named test_object containing two primitive shapes.
3. Record the object's initial global pose.
4. Construct a moveit_msgs::msg::CollisionObject with:
   - id = "test_object"
   - operation = CollisionObject::MOVE
   - A new global object pose different from the original pose.
   - Only one entry in primitive_poses, despite the existing object containing two shapes.
5. Submit the MOVE message through PlanningScene::processCollisionObjectMsg().
6. Check the returned status.
7. Retrieve test_object from the collision world and compare its global pose with the original pose.

The shape pose count mismatch should trigger the validation failure in processCollisionObjectMove().

### Expected behavior

When a MOVE request contains an invalid number of shape poses, the operation should be rejected without modifying the existing collision object.

The function should return false, and both the global object pose and individual shape poses should remain unchanged.

Failed MOVE operations should not leave the PlanningScene in a partially modified state.

### Actual behavior

Source inspection shows that processCollisionObjectMove() updates the global object pose before checking whether the number of supplied shape poses matches the number of shapes in the existing object.

When the shape pose count does not match, the function logs an error and returns false. However, the earlier call to world_->setObjectPose() has already been executed.

Therefore, the function can report failure while leaving the collision object's global pose modified.

This behavior is supported by the current source code, but a runtime regression test has not yet been executed.

### Description

In PlanningScene::processCollisionObjectAdd(), an existing collision object is removed before the replacement object's geometry is validated.

Affected file:

moveit_core/planning_scene/src/planning_scene.cpp

When an ADD operation targets an existing collision object, the following code removes the original object:

if (object.operation == moveit_msgs::msg::CollisionObject::ADD && world_->hasObject(object.id))
  world_->removeObject(object.id);

However, the replacement geometry is only parsed and validated afterward:

const Eigen::Isometry3d& world_to_object_header_transform =
    getFrameTransform(object.header.frame_id);

Eigen::Isometry3d header_to_pose_transform;
std::vector<shapes::ShapeConstPtr> shapes;
EigenSTL::vector_Isometry3d shape_poses;

if (!shapesAndPosesFromCollisionObjectMessage(
        object, header_to_pose_transform, shapes, shape_poses))
  return false;

const Eigen::Isometry3d object_frame_transform =
    world_to_object_header_transform * header_to_pose_transform;

world_->addToObject(object.id, object_frame_transform, shapes, shape_poses);

The geometry conversion function can return false when the input contains an invalid number of shape poses.

For example, if primitive_poses.size() exceeds primitives.size(), the conversion fails.

As a result, a malformed replacement ADD request can remove an existing valid collision object and then return false without restoring it.

This creates a partial state update and may cause an obstacle to disappear from the collision world even though the replacement operation failed.

In applications that rely on the PlanningScene for collision checking, this could lead to an incomplete representation of the environment.

Suggested Fix

Validate and construct the replacement geometry before removing the existing collision object.

The original object should remain unchanged if validation fails.

A regression test should verify that a rejected replacement ADD operation preserves the existing collision object and its geometry.

Humble

### OS and version

Ubuntu 22.04

### Source or binary build?

Source

None

### Steps to Reproduce

Proposed reproduction steps (not yet executed):

1. Create a PlanningScene instance with a valid robot model.
2. Add a valid collision object with the ID test_object, containing one primitive shape.
3. Verify that test_object exists in the collision world.
4. Construct a new moveit_msgs::msg::CollisionObject message with:
   - id = "test_object"
   - operation = CollisionObject::ADD
   - The same valid header.frame_id as the original object.
   - One primitive shape.
   - Two entries in primitive_poses, intentionally creating a mismatch between the number of shapes and poses.
5. Submit the replacement message using PlanningScene::processCollisionObjectMsg().
6. Check the return value of the operation.
7. Query the collision world using getWorld()->hasObject("test_object").

The mismatched shape and pose counts should cause 
shapesAndPosesFromCollisionObjectMessage() to return false after the existing object has already been removed.

### Expected behavior

When a replacement ADD message contains invalid geometry data, the operation should fail without modifying the existing collision object.

The original object should remain in the collision world with its geometry, pose, and associated state unchanged.

A failed replacement operation should not remove an existing valid obstacle from the PlanningScene.

### Actual behavior

Source inspection shows that processCollisionObjectAdd() removes the existing collision object before validating the replacement geometry.

If shapesAndPosesFromCollisionObjectMessage() detects an invalid shape/pose count, it returns false, causing processCollisionObjectAdd() to terminate without adding the replacement object.

Consequently, the original collision object can be removed even though the replacement ADD operation reports failure.

This behavior is supported by the source-level control flow but has not yet been verified by a runtime regression test.

new_candidates.body:
### Description

In moveit_core/collision_detection/src/world.cpp, World::knowsTransform() and World::getTransform() use different search behaviors when resolving subframes belonging to collision objects.

In World::knowsTransform() (around lines 156–164), the function returns immediately after finding the first object whose ID matches the prefix of the requested frame name:

for (const auto& object : objects_)
{
  if (name.rfind(object.first, 0) == 0 &&
      name[object.first.length()] == '/')
  {
    return object.second->global_subframe_poses_.find(
               name.substr(object.first.length() + 1)) !=
           object.second->global_subframe_poses_.end();
  }
}

However, World::getTransform() (around lines 191–203) continues searching other objects if a matching object does not contain the requested subframe:

for (const auto& object : objects_)
{
  if (name.rfind(object.first, 0) == 0 &&
      name[object.first.length()] == '/')
  {
    const auto it = object.second->global_subframe_poses_.find(
        name.substr(object.first.length() + 1));

    if (it != object.second->global_subframe_poses_.end())
    {
      return it->second;
    }
  }
}

As a result, when object IDs have overlapping prefixes, knowsTransform() may return false even though getTransform() can successfully resolve the requested frame.

For example, consider two collision objects:

- Object A: ID robot, without a subframe named tool/tip
- Object B: ID robot/tool, with a subframe named tip

When querying robot/tool/tip, both object IDs match the prefix condition.

Since objects_ is ordered by object ID, knowsTransform() can examine robot first and return false immediately, whereas getTransform() can continue searching and find tip under robot/tool.

This leads to inconsistent frame availability checks.

The example depends on slash-containing object IDs being accepted. This input condition should be verified against the intended API contract.

Suggested Fix

Make World::knowsTransform() consistent with World::getTransform() by continuing the search if the matching object does not contain the requested subframe.

Alternatively, enforce an unambiguous naming policy if overlapping object IDs are not intended to be supported.

Add regression tests for overlapping object-name prefixes and consistent frame lookup results.

### ROS Distro

Humble

### OS and version

Ubuntu 22.04

### Source or binary build?

Source

### If binary, which release version?

_No response_

### If source, which branch?

_No response_

### Which RMW are you using?

None

### Steps to Reproduce

Proposed reproduction steps (not yet executed):

1. Create a collision_detection::World instance.

2. Add two collision objects with the following configurations:

   Object A:
   - Object ID: robot
   - No subframe named tool/tip

   Object B:
   - Object ID: robot/tool
   - Subframe name: tip
   - Subframe transform: Identity

3. Query the following frame:

   const std::string frame = "robot/tool/tip";

   bool known = world.knowsTransform(frame);

   bool found = false;
   const Eigen::Isometry3d& transform =
       world.getTransform(frame, found);

4. Compare known and found.

5. Verify whether the API permits object IDs containing `/`, since this is required for the overlapping-prefix scenario.

Based on the source-level lookup logic, known may be false while found is true.

### Expected behavior

World::knowsTransform() and World::getTransform() should behave consistently when checking whether a requested transform exists.

If getTransform() can successfully resolve a subframe transform, knowsTransform() should also return true.

A prefix match should not cause the lookup to terminate unless the requested subframe has actually been found.

If overlapping object IDs are unsupported, the API should reject or document such names consistently.

### Actual behavior

Source inspection reveals inconsistent lookup behavior between the two methods.

World::knowsTransform() returns immediately after finding the first object ID matching the requested frame prefix, regardless of whether that object contains the requested subframe.

In contrast, World::getTransform() continues searching other matching objects if the requested subframe is not present.

For overlapping object ID prefixes, this may result in knowsTransform() returning false while getTransform() successfully resolves the transform.

This discrepancy has been identified through source inspection. Runtime reproduction has not yet been performed.

### Backtrace or Console output

_No response_

new_candidates.body:
### Description

In PlanningScene::shapesAndPosesFromCollisionObjectMessage(), failed geometry conversions can be silently skipped while the function still reports success.

Affected file:

moveit_core/planning_scene/src/planning_scene.cpp

The function uses shapes::constructShapeFromMsg() to convert geometry messages into internal Shape objects.

Inside the local append lambda (around lines 1841–1845), a null Shape pointer causes an immediate return:

```
auto append = [&object_pose, &shapes, &shape_poses,
               &switch_object_pose_and_shape_pose](
                  shapes::Shape* s,
                  const geometry_msgs::msg::Pose& pose_msg) {
  if (!s)
    return;

  // Process the successfully constructed shape.
};
```


This means that when constructShapeFromMsg() fails and returns nullptr, the corresponding geometry is omitted from the output.

However, after processing the primitive, mesh, and plane arrays, the enclosing function unconditionally returns true (around lines 1887–1890):


```
treat_shape_vectors(object.primitives, object.primitive_poses,
                    std::string("primitive_poses"));

treat_shape_vectors(object.meshes, object.mesh_poses,
                    std::string("meshes"));

treat_shape_vectors(object.planes, object.plane_poses,
                    std::string("planes"));

return true;
```


There is no final check to ensure that the number of successfully constructed shapes matches the number of input shapes.

Consequently, a collision object containing both valid and invalid geometry may be partially accepted without reporting the failed conversion to the caller.

In a motion-planning context, silently omitted geometry could cause the collision world to represent an incomplete obstacle.

This is a potential consequence of the source-level behavior, not a demonstrated physical collision.

Suggested Fix

Track whether any call to constructShapeFromMsg() fails.

If a geometry conversion fails, return an appropriate error status instead of silently omitting the shape, unless partial acceptance is explicitly intended and documented.

Add regression tests covering mixed valid and invalid geometry messages, including checks that the reported operation result matches the geometry actually stored in the collision world.

### ROS Distro

Humble

### OS and version

Ubuntu 22.04

### Source or binary build?

Source

### If binary, which release version?

_No response_

### If source, which branch?

_No response_

### Which RMW are you using?

None

### Steps to Reproduce

Proposed reproduction steps (not yet executed):

1. Create a PlanningScene with a valid robot model.

2. Construct a moveit_msgs::msg::CollisionObject with:
   - id = "test_object"
   - operation = CollisionObject::ADD
   - A valid header frame.
   - One valid primitive shape.
   - One malformed primitive shape for which shapes::constructShapeFromMsg() returns nullptr.
   - Corresponding primitive poses.

3. Submit the message through PlanningScene::processCollisionObjectMsg().

4. Check the returned success status.

5. Retrieve test_object from the collision world.

6. Compare the number of input shapes with the number of shapes actually stored in the world.

7. Verify whether the invalid geometry was skipped even though the operation reported success.

A concrete malformed shape message that reliably produces nullptr still needs to be identified and tested.

### Expected behavior

If any geometry conversion fails, the collision object processing operation should clearly report the failure.

The PlanningScene should not silently accept incomplete collision geometry while reporting that the entire operation succeeded.

Ideally, invalid geometry should cause the operation to fail without committing a partially constructed collision object.

Alternatively, if partial geometry acceptance is intentional, the behavior should be explicitly documented and communicated to the caller.

### Actual behavior

Source inspection shows that the append lambda immediately returns when constructShapeFromMsg() produces a null Shape pointer.

The failed geometry is therefore not added to the output shapes vector.

However, shapesAndPosesFromCollisionObjectMessage() returns true after processing the input geometry arrays, without checking whether all input shapes were successfully converted.

Consequently, the function may report success even when some input geometry has been omitted.

This behavior has been identified through source inspection. A runtime reproduction with malformed geometry has not yet been performed.

### Backtrace or Console output

_No response_
